GOV.UK press release (Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government): 'Clampdown on dangerous homes to protect more tenants and families'. JSON-LD datePublished = dateModified = 2026-10-08T22:30:02+01:00 (22:30 BST Thursday) - inside the window, after the 18:21 evening edition.
Awaab's Law to be extended to private renters; government consultation now open on how to implement it.
HARD FIGURES: 'Over 5 million more households could benefit'. Extending Awaab's Law to additional housing types 'could more than double the number of households protected by new timescales for repairs - from 4 million to around 9 million homes'. England has 11 million private renters. 'Around one in 10 private rented homes have a hazard at the most serious level (category 1)'. The Renters' Rights Act recently introduced fines of up to £7,000 where serious dangers are found.
CONSULTATION CLOSES 18 December 2026. It also covers whether to extend the law to temporary accommodation for homeless people and families, accommodation for young people leaving care, and supported housing for elderly and disabled people.
Awaab's Law came in for social housing last year, in memory of two-year-old Awaab Ishak, who died in 2020 after prolonged exposure to dangerous damp and mould.
Housing Minister Matthew Pennycook: 'Irrespective of tenure, all renters have the right to live in a safe and decent home and have complaints responded to in a timely manner. Awaab's Law is already helping to drive up standards in the social housing sector. We're now moving to extend it to private landlords so that England's 11 million private renters can enjoy the same protections.'
Holly Williamson, Chief Executive of Generation Rent: 'Homes are the foundations of our lives. But too many renters live in homes that are harmful to our health and often wait months for landlords to act on issues. We're pleased to see the government moving forward with bringing in Awaab's Law. It must be put in action as soon as possible to make sure every renter can live in a good quality home.'
Francesca Albanese, Director of Policy & Social Change at Crisis: 'With millions of people renting privately across England, it's crucial that tenants have a safe place to call home and that hazards like damp and mould are dealt with quickly.'
Clara Collingwood, Director of the Renters' Reform Coalition: 'A home should be a place of safety, and nobody in the UK should have to live in a home that is making them ill or putting their lives at risk, regardless of whether they rent their home from the council or from private landlords.'
Commitments sit in the Renters' Rights Act and the National Plan to End Homelessness.
